site: Great Zimbabwe (great_zimbabwe, chapter 9, Africa and the Indian Ocean): the Great Enclosure and its conical tower, near Masvingo, Zimbabwe, 20.27 S 30.93 E (the atlas coordinates match the site). The Great Enclosure's outer wall is generally dated to the 14th century, within the site's 11th to 15th century occupation. It was built by the ancestors of Shona-speaking people.
view: Stand inside the Great Enclosure, on open ground about 15 to 25 m west or north-west of the conical tower, at standing eye height. Look toward the tower and the south-east stretch of the outer wall behind it. In frame: the conical tower at full height, left of centre, standing on bare ground. The much smaller ruined second tower stands beside it; check which side on a measured plan (see contested). Behind both, the inside face of the outer wall curves across the whole width of the plate. Its top is flat, and it stands close behind the tower and is taller than it, so its top edge lands near the tower's top in the picture, either just above it or just below it. A strip of brochure sky sits over the wall, with the crowns of one or two woodland trees beyond it. Cropped: the wall runs out of both sides of the frame. The Hill Complex lies north, behind and to the left of the viewer, and the wall would hide it anyway, so it is out of frame. The chevron frieze is on the outer face of the wall and cannot be seen from this spot. Optional, and only if the measured plan confirms it can be seen from here: the rounded end of the older inner wall, with the narrow dark slot of the Parallel Passage between it and the outer wall. Why this view: it is the only view in which the tower is not hidden. Outside, near the tower, the wall is taller than the tower and stands close to it, so the tower cannot be seen over it. This is the view most photographs of the tower take: tower against wall. It is also the view the ruling allows (walls, passage and tower). And at 92 x 70 it reads as a silhouette: a tapering, flat-topped cone against a long flat-topped band.

elements.fact: A solid, tapering tower of dry granite. It is about 9 to 10 m tall and about 5.5 m across at the base, narrowing to roughly 2 m at the top (sources differ slightly; see contested). It is a truncated cone with a flat, slightly ragged top: not pointed, not domed. It has no door, window, stair, ledge or internal chamber, and digging around and under it found none. It stands inside the enclosure, close to the south-east stretch of the outer wall. Its courses are regular and horizontal.

It exists and stands beside the great tower. It is much smaller and its top has fallen. My recollection of the standard photographs is that it stands well under half the great tower's height. Its exact size and which side it stands on are not verified here (see contested).

elements.element: Outer wall of the Great Enclosure, seen from the inside
elements.fact: Dry-stone granite with no mortar. It is up to about 11 m high, which makes it taller than the tower, and up to about 5 to 6 m thick at the base. It runs about 250 m around, and its highest and best-built stretch is the south-east one, near the tower. The faces are battered, leaning back as they rise. The wall curves in plan and has no corners. Its top is flat. This is Whitty's 'Q' style: the most regular coursing on the site.

Local granite, split from the exfoliating granite domes into roughly rectangular, brick-to-block-sized pieces. They are laid in thin, continuous horizontal courses with dry joints: no mortar and no plaster. The joints read as fine dark lines.

elements.element: Inner wall end and Parallel Passage (optional)
elements.fact: A narrow passage, about one person wide, runs between the outer wall and an older, rougher inner wall ('P' style). It leads from the north entrance to the area around the conical tower. Where a wall ends at an opening, the end is rounded, never square. Paint it only if the measured plan shows it can be seen from the chosen standpoint.

Not in frame. A band of zigzag coursing runs near the top of the outer face of the outer wall, along only the south-east/east stretch, about 52 m of the roughly 250 m circuit. From inside the enclosure it cannot be seen. The chevron is not the same pattern as dentelle, which is a single course of stones set on edge at an angle, like saw teeth.
Open, level ground of grey-tan granite sand with short grass. The interior was dug over and cleared of deposits by Hall in 1902 to 1904. No paving.
The site lies in miombo savanna woodland on the plateau at about 1,100 m, with broad-leaved trees such as msasa. No palms, no rainforest, no desert.
The set's shared brochure sky. Take a dry-season clear day, which is the tourist season.
The granite hill with walls and boulders, north of the Great Enclosure. It is the revered locus and stays out of frame (gate 6).

mustBeRight: One large tower: a truncated cone with a flat top. It is not pointed and not domed.
The large tower is about 1.6 to 1.8 times as tall as it is wide at the base.
The tower tapers evenly from base to top.
The tower has no door, window, stair, ledge or opening anywhere.
A second, much smaller tower stands beside the large one, lower and broken off at the top.
The towers stand inside the enclosure, in front of the inside face of the outer wall.
The outer wall's top edge in the picture is at or above the large tower's mid-height. The wall is never drawn as a low parapet with the tower rising far above it.
The outer wall curves across the frame and has a flat top.
The wall faces lean back as they rise. They are not vertical.
No square corners anywhere. Any wall end in view is rounded.
All stonework is shown as thin horizontal courses of small rectangular blocks.
No mortar lines, no plaster, no large ashlar blocks.
The granite reads as warm pale grey with darker streaks. It is not blue-grey and not yellow sandstone.
There is no chevron or zigzag pattern on the tower or on the inside face of the wall.
No hill, rocky outcrop or boulders appear on the skyline.
No bird carvings and no stone pillars with carvings on them.
No people, no offerings, no ritual objects.
The trees beyond the wall are broad-leaved savanna trees. No palms.
deliberatelyWrong: No visitors, guides, walkways, signs, ropes or site museum. The brochure clears the site of everything modern.

The interior is shown as clean ground and short grass. The inner walls, platforms, remains of clay house floors, and plants growing on the walls are left out so that the tower and wall read at 92 x 70.
Courses are suggested, not counted. The real coursing is too fine to show course by course at this size, so the bands are fewer and bolder than the real ones.
The stone is cleaned up. Lichen, rust staining and rain streaks are reduced to a few accents, as a brochure's printing would.

The light is the set's fixed upper-right sun, not the sun's true position for this standpoint and date. With the viewer facing roughly south-east it happens to be plausible for a summer afternoon, but it was not computed.
The wall's curve is simplified to one clean sweep, and later repairs and reconstructed stretches are not told apart from original fabric.

lighting: Bright, clear dry-season sun from the upper right (B.LIGHT). The round tower gets a lit right flank and a shaded left flank with a soft terminator, and the upper edge of each course picks up a thin highlight over a dark joint. The tower's top is lit. The inside face of the curving wall darkens from lit to shaded as it turns away from the light. The tower may cast a shadow to the left onto the ground and onto the wall behind it (B.castShadow). Shadows are the set's cool violet (B.C.shadow mixed in), never black. With the viewer facing roughly south-east, a sun to the right and above matches a summer afternoon sun in the west-south-west. The set's convention decides the light; this is only a sanity check, not a computed position.
pitfalls: Painting the tower as a pointed cone, a spire or a beehive dome. It is a flat-topped truncated cone.
Showing the tower from outside, rising over a low wall. The outer wall near it is taller than the tower and stands close to it.
Mortar lines, big squared blocks, or plastered walls. This is dry stone: small blocks in thin courses.
Adding a door, a window, a stair or a doorway at the base of the tower. It is solid.
Square corners or vertical wall faces. The walls curve in plan, have rounded ends and lean back as they rise.
Putting the chevron on the tower, on the inside face of the wall, or all the way round the wall. It runs only along the top of the outer face of the south-east/east stretch.
Treating chevron and dentelle as the same pattern (the task brief calls them 'chevron (dentelle)'). Chevron is a zigzag band. Dentelle is a single course of stones set at an angle, like saw teeth.
Drawing the small tower as a near-twin of the large one. It is much smaller and ruined.
Cold blue-grey granite, or a yellow sandstone warmth borrowed from Egypt. It is warm pale grey with dark streaks.
Putting the Hill Complex or its boulders on the horizon because they are famous. The ruling keeps them out of frame.
A soapstone Zimbabwe Bird on a pillar as a flourish. It is excluded, and none came from the Great Enclosure in any case.

Anything Near Eastern, Phoenician or Sabaean in the styling, or 'King Solomon's Mines' romance: no temple framing, no altar, no exotic figures, no palms, no jungle. A real mid-century Rhodesian brochure would have printed that myth. This one must not.
Using the nineteenth-century plates' captions or text. Only the drawings and photographs are reference, as the site looked in 1891 to 1905. Bent's and Hall's text attributes the builders wrongly.
gate6: The arc does not name the revered locus. The literature points to the Hill Complex: the granite hill north of the Great Enclosure, formerly called the 'Acropolis', with its caves and its Eastern Enclosure. Local Shona communities treat it as sacred. Oral tradition connects the Hill's cave to the voice of the ancestors and to rain-making, and the Eastern Enclosure is where the soapstone birds stood. Ndoro (2001, 2005) documents local communities treating the whole site as a shrine, not only a monument ('Your Monument, Our Shrine'), and names the Nemanwa, Mugabe and Charumbira clans with ceremonies there. The vignette must not show: (1) the Hill Complex in any form, including the hill, its walls, its balanced boulders, its caves and the Eastern Enclosure; (2) any soapstone Zimbabwe Bird or carved stone pillar (sacred objects, repatriated, and the national emblem); (3) any ceremony, offering, beer or snuff pot, spirit medium, or praying or kneeling figure; (4) any grave, burial or human remains; (5) any people at all. The Great Enclosure's outer wall, the Parallel Passage and the two towers are inside the ruling. Also do not use Bent's name 'the Temple' for the Great Enclosure, or anything that turns the enclosure into a shrine (an altar, offerings at the tower's foot). Note: I could not re-read Ndoro online in this run, so the clan names and the specific traditions come from the literature as I know it.
contested: Tower dimensions: commonly cited as about 9 m (30 ft) tall, sometimes about 10 m, and about 5.5 m across the base, narrowing to about 2 m. Some of the difference may be lost top courses. Keep the proportions and do not paint to an exact metre.

Outer wall: about 11 m is the usual maximum height, though some accounts give about 10 m. Thickness up to about 5 to 6 m at the base, circuit about 250 m. The figures vary by author and by the stretch measured.

What the conical tower was for: a symbolic granary standing for a ruler's tribute and generosity (the reading Garlake reports, following Shona tradition); a male or phallic symbol tied to initiation (Huffman 1996); a lookout. None is proven. Paint nothing that implies a use.
What the Great Enclosure was for: a royal residence or the royal wives' quarters (Garlake 1973), or an initiation school (domba, Huffman 1996). The colonial-era 'Temple' reading is rejected.

What the chevron means: Huffman ties it to male authority and rain, and others differ. Its position (the south-east/east outer face, about 52 m long) is not in dispute, but I have not re-checked the length here.

Chronology: Huffman and Vogel (1991) give a sequence of Hill, then Great Enclosure, then Valley. Chirikure et al. (2013, Bayesian model) argue that construction overlapped. The Great Enclosure's outer wall is usually put in the 14th century.
The name: 'dzimba dza mabwe' (houses of stone) or 'dzimba woye' (venerated houses, used of chiefs' houses or graves). Both derivations are current.

Unverified, not disputed. The second tower's height and which side of the great tower it stands on: the current code draws it at about half the great tower's height, which may be too large. Check a measured plan (Caton-Thompson 1931, Garlake 1973, the NMMZ plan) before painting.
Unverified, not disputed. Whether the tower's top had a decorative course that has since fallen. Paint the top plain and slightly ragged.

Unverified, not disputed. Early accounts report monoliths and small turrets on the top of the outer wall above the chevron stretch. Whether any stand where they could be seen from inside is unchecked. Leave the wall top plain unless the check confirms them.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage List 364: Great Zimbabwe National Monument (inscribed 1986)
sources.detail: Site authority for identity, dates and the site's significance. Fetching it in this run was refused by the egress proxy, so it was cited, not re-read.

sources.title: Peter S. Garlake, Great Zimbabwe (London: Thames and Hudson, 1973); and Great Zimbabwe Described and Explained (Harare, 1982)
sources.detail: Standard archaeological description: Great Enclosure dimensions, the conical tower and small tower, the Parallel Passage, the chevron on the south-east outer wall, the royal-residence interpretation. Source for the main figures. Copyright; reference only.

sources.title: Gertrude Caton-Thompson, The Zimbabwe Culture: Ruins and Reactions (Oxford: Clarendon, 1931)
sources.detail: British Association excavation of 1929. Settled that the builders were African, with measured plans and sections of the Great Enclosure and tower. Not public domain (US public domain only from 1 January 2027; UK and EU 2056). Use for measurements on screen only.

sources.title: David Randall-MacIver, Mediaeval Rhodesia (London: Macmillan, 1906)
sources.detail: First professional excavation (1905). Argued for African builders and a medieval date against Bent and Hall. Photographs and plans are public domain. The preferred public-domain visual reference, and its text is right.

sources.title: J. Theodore Bent, The Ruined Cities of Mashonaland (London: Longmans, 1892), with plans by R. M. W. Swan
sources.detail: Public-domain plates of the tower and walls as they stood in 1891, before Hall's clearance. The text is the documented Phoenician/Arab misattribution: use the drawings only, never the text.

sources.title: R. N. Hall, Great Zimbabwe, Mashonaland, Rhodesia (London: Methuen, 1905); Hall and Neal, The Ancient Ruins of Rhodesia (1902)
sources.detail: Public-domain photographs of the conical tower and enclosure. Hall's 1902 to 1904 clearance destroyed deposits inside the Great Enclosure. His text is the foreign-builder error; use only as a picture of the ruin c. 1902.

sources.title: Carl Mauch, journals and plans of 1871, published in Petermanns Geographische Mitteilungen, Ergänzungsheft 37 (1874)
sources.detail: Earliest European plan and sketches of the ruins. Public domain. His Queen of Sheba attribution is the first of the foreign-builder claims and is excluded.

sources.title: Anthony Whitty, 'The origins of the stone architecture of Zimbabwe', Proceedings of the First Federal Science Congress (Salisbury, 1961)
sources.detail: The P, Q and R wall styles: Q is the regular coursing of the Great Enclosure's outer wall and the tower; P is the older, rougher inner wall.

sources.title: Thomas N. Huffman, Snakes and Crocodiles: Power and Symbolism in Ancient Zimbabwe (Johannesburg: Witwatersrand University Press, 1996)
sources.detail: Symbolic readings of the Great Enclosure (initiation), the tower and the chevron. Cited for the disputes, not as settled fact.

sources.title: Webber Ndoro, Your Monument Our Shrine: The Preservation of Great Zimbabwe (Uppsala, Studies in African Archaeology 19, 2001); and ICCROM Conservation Studies 4 (2005)
sources.detail: Local communities' spiritual relationship to the site, the sacred standing of the Hill Complex, and conservation of the walls (lichen, plant growth, reconstruction). Basis for the gate-6 answer. Not re-read in this run.

sources.title: Innocent Pikirayi, The Zimbabwe Culture: Origins and Decline of Southern Zambezian States (AltaMira, 2001); Chirikure and Pikirayi, 'Inside and outside the dry stone walls', Antiquity 82 (2008)
sources.detail: Current synthesis of construction, function and dating.

sources.title: Chirikure, Pollard, Manyanga and Bandama, 'A Bayesian chronology for Great Zimbabwe', Antiquity 87 (2013); Huffman and Vogel, 'The chronology of Great Zimbabwe', South African Archaeological Bulletin 46 (1991)
sources.detail: The two sides of the construction-sequence dispute.

repoCorrections: content/map/README.md, vignettes table, chapter 9 row, 'The conical tower seen over the enclosure wall': from outside this cannot be seen. The outer wall beside the tower, up to about 11 m, is taller than the tower (about 9 to 10 m) and stands close to it. The row should say the tower is seen from inside the Great Enclosure, standing in front of the inside face of the outer wall. The rest of the row is right: the smaller second tower that has largely fallen; dry stone, no mortar, no door, no stair, solid.
src/map/monuments.ts, 'conical-tower' doc comment, 'seen over the outer wall': the same error.

src/map/monuments.ts, 'conical-tower', proportions: the wall is drawn in front of the towers with its top at y of about 51 to 56 over a ground at y 72, while the great tower rises to y of about 12. That makes the tower about three times the height of a wall that is actually taller than it. The wall should be behind the towers, with its top at or above the tower's mid-height.
src/map/monuments.ts, 'conical-tower', summit: the great tower's top is drawn as a dome raised 4 units above the shoulders (quadraticCurveTo). The real tower is flat-topped (truncated).

src/map/monuments.ts, 'conical-tower', small tower: drawn at about half the great tower's height and 60% of its base width. On the standard photographs it looks much smaller than that. Check a measured plan and resize.

content/research/arc.md section 7, 'any pre-Bent attribution of Great Zimbabwe to Phoenicians or Sheba': read literally, this excludes only claims made before Bent. The exclusion should cover every foreign-builder attribution: Mauch 1871 (Sheba), Bent 1892 (Phoenician/Arab), Hall 1902 to 1905 (Phoenician/Sabaean), and the Rhodesian-era guidebooks that repeated them. Randall-MacIver (1906) and Caton-Thompson (1931) are the correction.

content/research/arc.md chapter 9 table, Great Zimbabwe row, 'Hill Complex on kopje, 11 m drystone wall, conical tower': the 11 m wall belongs to the Great Enclosure, not the Hill Complex. The row also leads with the Hill Complex, the part the 2026-09-23 ruling puts out of frame. The row, or the ruling, should name the revered locus as the Hill Complex, with its caves, the Eastern Enclosure and the birds, so that no later designer has to guess.

content/research/arc.md chapter 9 imagery line and section 6: for Great Zimbabwe specifically there is public-domain imagery beyond 'Bent 1892': Mauch 1871 to 1874, Hall 1902 and 1905, and Randall-MacIver 1906. Randall-MacIver is the one whose text is also right. The 'weakest in the game' rating fits the coastal sites, not this one.
confidence: Medium for the descriptive facts, low for the exact figures. Nothing was checked on the web in this run. The first WebSearch call returned 'budget exhausted (200 of 200 searches used this session)'. WebFetch was refused by the egress proxy for every domain tried: whc.unesco.org, en.wikipedia.org, britannica.com, zimfieldguide.com, archive.org, gutenberg.org, books.google.com, commons.wikimedia.org, smarthistory.org, metmuseum.org, uu.diva-portal.org, journals.plos.org, cambridge.org, worldhistory.org and sahistory.org.za. Everything above comes from the standard literature listed in sources as I know it, cited by title and not re-read. The following are widely agreed across that literature: dry-stone granite with no mortar; battered, curving walls with rounded ends; a solid, flat-topped tower with no opening; a second, smaller ruined tower; the chevron on the outer face of the south-east stretch; a wall taller than the tower; the Hill Complex as the sacred focus; and African builders. Check these against Garlake 1973 or Caton-Thompson 1931 and the NMMZ site plan before the asset note is committed: the numbers (tower 9 to 10 m by 5.5 m; wall up to 11 m high, about 250 m around, up to 5 to 6 m thick; chevron about 52 m); the small tower's size and side; any monoliths on the wall top; the tower's summit; and whether the Parallel Passage mouth can be seen from the chosen standpoint. I recommend repeating the web checks when egress and search budget are available, and before painting starts.
